methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a single-site cross-sectional convenience sample recruited from one healthcare system's EDW, with all exposures and outcomes self-reported, limiting internal validity and generalizability (acknowledged in the limitations). Of 736 participants who completed a portion of the questionnaire, only 518 had complete data for the analyses, yet the manuscript provides no description of missing-data mechanisms or imputation strategy and no CONSORT/flow-style accounting of exclusions. The analytic approach is restricted to univariate logistic regressions across three outcomes and roughly 15 predictors each (≈45 tests), with no multivariable adjustment for confounding (e.g., age, income, education all tested separately though clearly correlated) and no multiplicity correction, which inflates the risk of spurious associations. No a priori power calculation is reported, endpoints are convenience measures rather than validated psychometric instruments (apart from the modified Godin), and sensitivity analyses are absent.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a cross-sectional observational survey of post-treatment cancer survivors from a single health system, mapping to Oxford LoE 4 (low-quality cohort / cross-sectional survey). The clinical question — who among cancer survivors owns and uses mHealth tools and is willing to share wearable data — is relevant to survivorship care implementation but the endpoints are purely descriptive (ownership, app use, willingness) rather than patient-relevant outcomes such as PA change, quality of life, OS, or PFS. The translational path is speculative: the paper outlines many potential EHR-integration strategies in the discussion, but the data themselves do not test any intervention or clinical workflow. Findings may help target future implementation studies but are unlikely to directly inform guidelines or practice.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable checklist for this cross-sectional observational study. Inclusion/exclusion criteria, variable definitions, recruitment window (April–June 2023), and setting (Northwestern Medicine EDW) are reported, and demographic/clinical descriptors are clearly tabulated — satisfying many core STROBE items. However, several items are weak or missing: no participant flow diagram, no explicit handling of the 218 participants excluded for incomplete data, no description of how potential confounding was addressed (indeed, only univariate models are used), no reporting of effect-size interpretation beyond ORs, and no sensitivity analyses. The manuscript provides no data-availability or code-availability statement in the retained text, no repository identifiers, and no supplementary materials sufficient for independent replication, which is a notable reproducibility gap.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is incremental: the manuscript explicitly compares its ownership estimates to prior HINTS-based analyses (Zhou 2024, Gitonga 2025) and acknowledges that higher-SES correlates of adoption have already been documented in connected-health technology studies among cancer survivors. The main empirical contribution is updating adoption prevalence to 2023 within a single health-system sample and disaggregating by specific apps/devices (MyFitnessPal, Peloton, Apple Watch, Fitbit). No new conceptual framework, novel measurement instrument, or underserved population is introduced; indeed the sample is predominantly White, educated, and higher income. The willingness-to-share-data analysis is somewhat less saturated in the literature, but the single significant correlate (full-time employment) limits the empirical yield.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable, with a clear IMRaD structure, defined acronyms (PA, MVPA, mHealth, CS, EDW), and an abstract that quantitatively reflects the headline findings. However, the discussion is disproportionately long and repetitive — the extended section proposing EHR-integration strategies, dashboards, nudges, and digital-literacy workshops reads more like a narrative review or editorial than discussion of the actual results, and dilutes the empirical message. One inconsistency: the abstract and results report 52.9% activity-tracker ownership, but the discussion states '56% [N = 518]' when comparing to prior studies, which should be reconciled. Captions for Tables 1 and 2 are terse and not standalone-interpretable from the text provided.

key_strengths: Timely 2023 health-system sample of 518 post-treatment survivors with disaggregation of specific apps and wearable brands
Clear operational definitions of predictors and outcomes, with ORs and 95% CIs consistently reported
Discussion thoughtfully links adoption disparities to equity-oriented implementation strategies
Readable IMRaD structure with abstract that quantitatively reflects findings
key_concerns: Analysis is restricted to univariate logistic regressions across ~45 tests without any multivariable adjustment or multiplicity correction, raising confounding and false-positive risks
No participant flow diagram or handling of the 218 excluded incomplete cases; missing-data mechanism unexamined
Single-site convenience sample, predominantly White/high-SES, strongly limiting generalizability — acknowledged but not mitigated
Internal inconsistency between 52.9% (results/abstract) and 56% (discussion) activity-tracker ownership figures should be reconciled
No data-availability or code-availability statement; outcomes are descriptive and not patient-relevant endpoints
Novelty is incremental over prior HINTS-based analyses and over similar health-system surveys
chief_reviewer.rationale: Competent but descriptive single-site cross-sectional survey with substantive analytic limitations (univariate-only, no multiplicity control, excluded cases unaccounted for) and incremental novelty. Appropriate for a Tier 4 journal with minor revisions to reconcile prevalence figures, add a flow diagram, and consider multivariable adjustment.
